A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Subjective Camera work, renamed Subjective Camera 0.1 in v2. All pages, equations, tables, figures and references support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original CMC/FMC benchmark results, qualitative ablations and a 30-participant user study in Section 4.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and reports a revised 40-participant user study, controlled preference experiments and a sketch-optimization case study.

M1.justification: The text-reward, sequential integration and sketch-refinement pipeline remains; SADG/LO correspond to CSO/SE. As written, v2's sketch initialization omits the explicit additive Gaussian term in v1 Equation (7). V2 also suggests rescaling small sketches or skipping their optimization. Its newly explicit alignment losses primarily specify roles already described in v1.

E1.justification: CMC and FMC retain their sources, tasks and sizes: 142 and 42 sketches. Human-evaluation coverage extends from participants judging their own recalled scenes to gallery-photo-based reconstructions assessed by both readout providers and independent observers, adding a distinct rater population and reference-based scenario.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, Uni-ControlNet, Multi-Sketch, PNP and FreeControl. The user-study comparator set changes: v2 evaluates text-reward-only and text-reward-plus-OP baselines alongside FreeControl, while v1's explicit no-text-reward, no-LO and shuffled-order comparisons disappear from that study.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 replaces FMC's LPIPS metric with CLIP-I; CLIP becomes CLIP-T without changing the shared scores. Section 4.4 replaces 30 participants completing three input-refinement rounds with 12 readout providers and 28 additional raters, photo-reference comparisons, four judgment questions and five-second versus unlimited reference-viewing conditions.

E4.justification: V1's drawing-order permutation test and three-round input-adaptation analysis disappear. V2 adds a sketch-optimization case study in Figure 4 and controls examining rater identity, reference exposure and judgment criteria in Figure 8. The basic module-ablation examples remain, moving from v1 Figure 4 to v2 Figure 6 with renamed components.

E5.justification: Both versions report point scores and preference percentages without seed counts, confidence intervals, repeated-run uncertainty or specified significance tests. V1's three rounds vary user inputs rather than estimate run variability. V2's statement that one advantage is not statistically significant supplies no new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: All 42 shared FID, CLIP/CLIP-T and HPS entries in Table 1 are equivalent after rounding. LPIPS entries are replaced by CLIP-I results, including 0.797 for Ours and 0.775 for FreeControl. Human-study outcomes are substantially replaced, including Q1 preference rates of 67.29% against FreeControl and 85.00% against text-reward-plus-OP. The changed protocols prevent direct comparison with v1's win rates.

T1.justification: V2 defines the appearance descriptor and explicit spatial, appearance and preservation losses in Equations (6) and (8–13), substantially specifying functions left abstract in v1 Equation (6). It also removes v1's explicit VAE covariance definition and exponential learning-rate recurrence. These change the mathematical specification; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free sequential reconstruction and benchmark superiority remain. V2 qualifies reconstruction capability by explicitly acknowledging imperfect scene recovery and dependence on sketch quality and order, whereas v1's conclusion presents those challenges as effectively addressed. The abstract also foregrounds user-preference evidence.

C2.justification: V2 adds small-sketch failure conditions, explains why unconstrained text-reward generation can be preferred for visual realism, and interprets rater and reference-exposure effects. Its conclusion attributes reconstruction errors to prior mismatch and discusses personalization and improved readouts. These substantially expand limitations and qualifications while replacing v1's interpretation of progressive user adaptation.

D1.justification: V2 names DDIM inversion/SDEdit options, describes linear-interpolation handling of small sketches and supplies a project-page address. It omits v1's explicit learning-rate decay setting mu=5.0 and dataset-release promise. Hardware, 512-by-512 inputs and shared coefficients remain. The PDFs alone do not establish actual code or dataset availability.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands from sketch generation and reward optimization to broader controllable synthesis, including layout guidance and image editing. Added works include Kosslyn's mental-imagery research, DyMO, Diffusion Self-Guidance and Block and Detail. V2 explicitly distinguishes reconstruction of experienced scenes from creative generation and credits existing text-reward optimization practice.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method overview and conclusion are extensively rewritten around subjective readouts and a physical-camera analogy. Contributions are reorganized, and the method now separates Sketch Encoding, Appearance Encoding and Concept-wise Sequential Optimization. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond terminology changes.

P2.justification: V2 introduces a new teaser and motivation figure, redraws the pipeline and adds the sketch-optimization illustration. It merges v1's CMC/FMC comparison grids into Figure 5 with color-coded sketch order, reformats the retained ablation display and Table 1, and replaces the user-study charts with new preference and control plots.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves technical assessability by defining central losses that v1 left unspecified. Photo-referenced user judgments, separate evaluation criteria and rater/exposure controls better support assessment of reconstruction fidelity, while explicit failure conditions temper broad claims. Removing direct order-shuffling and input-refinement evidence weakens support for those specific behaviors, and formal uncertainty remains absent. Nevertheless, the gains in method specification, evaluation relevance and interpretation constitute a substantial overall improvement.
